```{r libraries, message = FALSE}
library(nlmixr2lib)
library(rxode2)
library(PKNCA)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)

rxode2::rxSetSeed(20240708)
set.seed(20240708)
```

Wijk et al. (2024) studied whether alcohol and illicit substance use alter the
steady-state pharmacokinetics of the four first-line tuberculosis drugs in
adults starting treatment in Worcester, South Africa (the TRUST cohort). The
paper develops **four separate population PK models**, one per drug, and this
package ships them as four model files that share this vignette:

```{r load_models}
rif <- nlmixr2lib::readModelDb("Wijk_2024_rifampicin")
inh <- nlmixr2lib::readModelDb("Wijk_2024_isoniazid")
pza <- nlmixr2lib::readModelDb("Wijk_2024_pyrazinamide")
emb <- nlmixr2lib::readModelDb("Wijk_2024_ethambutol")
```

Reference: Wijk M, Gausi K, Malatesta S, Weber SE, Court R, Myers B, Carney T,
Parry CDH, Horsburgh CR, White LF, Wiesner L, Warren RM, Uren C, McIlleron H,
Kloprogge F, Denti P, Jacobson KR. The impact of alcohol and illicit substance
use on the pharmacokinetics of first-line TB drugs. *J Antimicrob Chemother*
2024;79(8):2022. [doi:10.1093/jac/dkae206](https://doi.org/10.1093/jac/dkae206)

The headline finding is negative: no clinically relevant effect of alcohol use
on any of the four drugs. The covariates that did survive are a 19% lower
rifampicin bioavailability with methaqualone (Mandrax) use, NAT2 acetylator
phenotype on isoniazid, creatinine clearance on ethambutol clearance, and
fat-free mass as the size descriptor for all four drugs.

## Population

| Characteristic | Median (IQR) or n (%) |
|---|---|
| Participants | 104 |
| Male | 73 (70%) |
| Age (years) | 37.0 (27.0-48.3) |
| Weight (kg) | 51.4 (45.5-56.9) |
| Fat-free mass (kg) | 43.1 (35.8-47.0) |
| Creatinine clearance (mL/min) | 128 (105-150) |
| Alcohol use low / moderate / high / missing | 30 (29%) / 44 (42%) / 29 (28%) / 1 (1%) |
| Methaqualone use (urine test) | 29 (28%) |
| NAT2 genotype available | 34 (33%): 32% slow, 41% intermediate, 27% fast |

Values reproduce Table 1 of the source. Participants were at least 15 years
old, without HIV, and had drug-susceptible pulmonary tuberculosis. They took
fixed-dose combination tablets once daily (rifampicin 150 mg, isoniazid 75 mg,
pyrazinamide 400 mg, ethambutol 275 mg per tablet) with the number of tablets
set by WHO weight band, and were sampled under fasting conditions 4-8 weeks
into treatment, pre-dose and at 1.5, 3, 5 and 8 h post-dose.

## Source trace

Every `ini()` value carries an in-file comment naming its source location. The
table below is the vignette-level summary.

| Quantity | Rifampicin | Isoniazid | Pyrazinamide | Ethambutol | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Disposition | 1-cmt, liver compartment | 2-cmt, algebraic liver | 1-cmt | 2-cmt | Results; supplementary control streams |
| Clearance (L/h, FFM 43.4 kg) | CLint,max*fu 42.5, Km 7 mg/L | CLint*fu 14.8 / 36.3 / 62.4 (slow / int. / fast) | 4.48 | 48.8 | Table 2 |
| Vc (L) | 55.1 | 59.3 | 41.4 | 233 | Table 2 |
| Vp (L), Q (L/h) | - | 38.2, 3.45 | - | 510, 34.4 | Table 2 |
| ka (1/h) | 1.82 | 3.28 (held constant) | 1.89 | 1.39 | Table 2 |
| MTT (h) | 0.689 | 0.681 | 0.289 | 0.451 | Table 2 |
| NN in KTR = (NN+1)/MTT | 17 | 0 | 2.73 | 2.01 | control streams (Table 2 prints 17, 1, 3.73, 3.01) |
| QH, VH (FFM 56.1 kg) | 90 L/h, 1 L | 90 L/h | - | - | Table 2 footnote d; control streams |
| Covariates | methaqualone on F (+19.2% in non-users) | NAT2 on CLint | 2.49-fold BOV for unobserved doses | CrCl on CL (+0.264% per mL/min) | control streams; Results |
| BSV on clearance | 35.2% | 29.3% | 20.3% | 16.3% | Table 2 |
| BOV on F / ka / MTT | 5.40 / 136 / 79.9% | 22.3 / 130 / 67.5% | 10.8 / 69.1 / 90.2% | 19.8 / 112 / 94.2% | Table 2 |
| Residual error | 13.7%, 0.0234 mg/L | 17.0%, 0.021 mg/L | 2.66%, 0.63 mg/L | 10.5%, 0.0169 mg/L | Table 2; control-stream `ADD = THETA + 0.2*LLOQ` |

The supplement reproduces the four final NONMEM control streams. Their
`$THETA` and `$OMEGA` blocks match Table 2 (rifampicin to within 0.3%, the
others to the printed digits), so the control streams supply structure and the
rows Table 2 omits, and Table 2 supplies the estimated values.

## Structural verification

These checks compare a solve against its own closed form with the same
parameters on both sides, so the only difference is numerical integration
error, and they are asserted tightly.

```{r gate_helpers}
trap <- function(time, conc) {
  sum(diff(time) * (utils::head(conc, -1) + utils::tail(conc, -1)) / 2)
}

# Once-daily oral doses into the absorption compartment, with a fine
# observation grid over the last dosing interval. Times are returned relative
# to the last dose.
daily_events <- function(amt, n_dose = 14, step = 0.01) {
  last <- 24 * (n_dose - 1)
  dose <- data.frame(time = 24 * (seq_len(n_dose) - 1), amt = amt, evid = 1,
                     cmt = "depot")
  obs <- data.frame(time = seq(last, last + 24, by = step), amt = NA_real_,
                    evid = 0, cmt = "central")
  ev <- rbind(dose, obs)
  ev[order(ev$time, -ev$evid), ]
}

typical_last_interval <- function(model, amt, covariates, n_dose = 14) {
  ev <- daily_events(amt, n_dose = n_dose)
  for (nm in names(covariates)) ev[[nm]] <- covariates[[nm]]
  out <- rxode2::rxSolve(rxode2::zeroRe(model), ev, returnType = "data.frame")
  out <- out[out$time >= 24 * (n_dose - 1), ]
  out$time <- out$time - 24 * (n_dose - 1)
  out
}
```

**Pyrazinamide and ethambutol: steady-state mass balance.** At steady state the
amount eliminated over one dosing interval equals the dose, so `CL * AUCtau`
must equal the administered amount. This pins the unit chain (mg, L, mg/L) and
confirms that the transit density delivers each dose exactly once. For
ethambutol the creatinine clearance is set to the 127.1 mL/min centring value
of the control stream (age 37 years and a serum creatinine back-solved from
it), so clearance takes its tabulated value of 48.8 L/h.

```{r gate_mass_balance}
creat_ref <- (140 - 37) * 52 * 88.4 / (72 * 127.1)

pza_ss <- typical_last_interval(pza, 1200, list(FFM = 43.4, OCC = 2, SELFADMIN = 0))
emb_ss <- typical_last_interval(
  emb, 3 * 275 * 0.74,
  list(FFM = 43.4, OCC = 2, AGE = 37, CREAT = creat_ref)
)

mass_balance <- c(
  pyrazinamide = 4.48 * trap(pza_ss$time, pza_ss$Cc) / 1200,
  ethambutol = 48.8 * trap(emb_ss$time, emb_ss$Cc) / (3 * 275 * 0.74)
)
stopifnot(abs(mass_balance - 1) < 1e-3)
mass_balance
```

**Isoniazid and rifampicin: the well-stirred liver identity.** With a
well-stirred liver, first-pass loss removes a fraction EH of the dose while
systemic hepatic clearance is QH * EH, and the two cancel: the apparent oral
clearance is exactly the unbound intrinsic clearance, whatever the hepatic
blood flow. For isoniazid this must hold for each NAT2 phenotype at steady
state. For rifampicin intrinsic clearance is saturable, so the identity holds
only in the linear limit; a 1 mg single dose keeps the liver concentration
far below Km = 7 mg/L, so dose / AUC must recover CLint,max * fu = 42.5 L/h in
a methaqualone user (F = 1) and 42.5 / 1.191955 L/h in a non-user.

```{r gate_well_stirred}
phenotypes <- data.frame(
  phenotype = c("Slow", "Intermediate", "Fast"),
  NAT2_SLOW = c(1, 0, 0),
  NAT2_RAPID = c(0, 0, 1),
  clint = c(14.8, 36.3, 62.4)
)
inh_ss <- lapply(seq_len(nrow(phenotypes)), function(i) {
  typical_last_interval(inh, 225, list(
    FFM = 43.4, OCC = 2,
    NAT2_SLOW = phenotypes$NAT2_SLOW[i], NAT2_RAPID = phenotypes$NAT2_RAPID[i]
  ))
})
phenotypes$oral_cl <- vapply(inh_ss, function(p) 225 / trap(p$time, p$Cc), numeric(1))

rif_lowdose <- function(methaqualone) {
  ev <- data.frame(
    time = c(0, seq(0, 72, by = 0.01)), amt = c(1, rep(NA, 7201)),
    evid = c(1, rep(0, 7201)), cmt = c("depot", rep("central", 7201)),
    FFM = 43.4, OCC = 2, CONMED_METHAQUALONE = methaqualone
  )
  out <- rxode2::rxSolve(rxode2::zeroRe(rif), ev, returnType = "data.frame")
  1 / trap(out$time, out$Cc)
}
rif_cl <- c(user = rif_lowdose(1), non_user = rif_lowdose(0))

stopifnot(
  max(abs(phenotypes$oral_cl / phenotypes$clint - 1)) < 1e-3,
  abs(rif_cl[["user"]] / 42.5 - 1) < 5e-3,
  abs(rif_cl[["non_user"]] / (42.5 / 1.191955) - 1) < 5e-3
)
phenotypes |>
  dplyr::select(-NAT2_SLOW, -NAT2_RAPID) |>
  dplyr::rename(
    "NAT2 phenotype" = phenotype,
    "CLint * fu (L/h)" = clint,
    "Dose / AUCtau from solve (L/h)" = oral_cl
  ) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3)
rif_cl
```

The rifampicin tolerance is wider than the others because the 1 mg dose still
saturates intrinsic clearance very slightly; the residual is a property of the
model, not of the integration.

**Rifampicin: saturable hepatic extraction.** Exposure rises more than
proportionally with dose because the liver concentration approaches Km. Over
the weight-band doses (2 to 5 tablets) the steady-state AUC per mg rises
monotonically:

```{r gate_rif_nonlinear}
rif_doses <- c(300, 450, 600, 750)
rif_auc <- vapply(rif_doses, function(d) {
  p <- typical_last_interval(rif, d, list(FFM = 43.4, OCC = 2, CONMED_METHAQUALONE = 0),
                             n_dose = 7)
  trap(p$time, p$Cc)
}, numeric(1))
dose_norm <- rif_auc / rif_doses
stopifnot(all(diff(dose_norm) > 0))
data.frame(dose = rif_doses, auc = rif_auc, auc_per_mg = dose_norm) |>
  dplyr::rename(
    "Daily dose (mg)" = dose,
    "AUCtau (mg*h/L)" = auc,
    "AUCtau per mg" = auc_per_mg
  ) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3)
```

## Virtual cohort

The cohort mirrors Table 1. Weight is log-normal around the 51.4 kg median with
the reported interquartile range; height is drawn by sex (not reported, so
typical South African adult heights are assumed); fat-free mass follows from
the Janmahasatian formula the control streams use. Each participant gets the
WHO weight-band number of fixed-dose combination tablets (2 tablets below
38 kg, 3 for 38-54 kg, 4 for 55-70 kg, 5 above 70 kg). Ethambutol enters the
model as ethambutol base, 0.74 times the 275 mg of dihydrochloride per tablet.

Methaqualone use is drawn at the observed 28%. NAT2 phenotype is drawn with the
mixture-model probabilities of 36% slow, 40% intermediate and 24% fast that the
authors used for participants without a genotype. Age and serum creatinine are
drawn so that the standardised Cockcroft-Gault creatinine clearance has a
median close to the 127.1 mL/min centring value.

Each participant takes seven daily doses. As in the study, the dose before the
PK day (with the pre-dose sample) is occasion 1 and the observed dose on the PK
day is occasion 2; earlier doses share occasion 1. For pyrazinamide the
occasion-1 doses are flagged as unobserved (`SELFADMIN = 1`), which inflates
their between-occasion variability 2.49-fold.

```{r cohort}
n_subj <- 150

sex_f <- stats::rbinom(n_subj, 1, 0.30)
wt <- pmin(pmax(stats::rlnorm(n_subj, log(51.4), 0.166), 32), 90)
ht <- ifelse(sex_f == 1, stats::rnorm(n_subj, 1.58, 0.06), stats::rnorm(n_subj, 1.69, 0.07))
ffm <- ifelse(
  sex_f == 1,
  37.99 * ht^2 * wt / (35.98 * ht^2 + wt),
  42.92 * ht^2 * wt / (30.93 * ht^2 + wt)
)
n_tab <- cut(wt, c(0, 38, 55, 71, Inf), right = FALSE, labels = FALSE) + 1

cohort <- data.frame(
  id = seq_len(n_subj), FFM = ffm, n_tab = n_tab,
  CONMED_METHAQUALONE = stats::rbinom(n_subj, 1, 0.28),
  nat2 = sample(c("Slow", "Intermediate", "Fast"), n_subj, replace = TRUE,
                prob = c(0.36, 0.40, 0.24)),
  AGE = pmin(pmax(stats::rlnorm(n_subj, log(37), 0.3), 15), 75),
  CREAT = stats::rlnorm(n_subj, log(52), 0.2)
)
cohort$NAT2_SLOW <- as.numeric(cohort$nat2 == "Slow")
cohort$NAT2_RAPID <- as.numeric(cohort$nat2 == "Fast")
cohort$crcl_std <- (140 - cohort$AGE) * 52 / (72 * cohort$CREAT / 88.4)

obs_times <- c(143.99, seq(144, 168, by = 0.1))

cohort_events <- function(mg_per_tablet) {
  dose <- data.frame(
    id = rep(cohort$id, each = 7), time = rep(24 * 0:6, n_subj),
    amt = rep(mg_per_tablet * cohort$n_tab, each = 7), evid = 1, cmt = "depot"
  )
  obs <- data.frame(
    id = rep(cohort$id, each = length(obs_times)), time = rep(obs_times, n_subj),
    amt = NA_real_, evid = 0, cmt = "central"
  )
  ev <- rbind(dose, obs)
  ev <- ev[order(ev$id, ev$time, -ev$evid), ]
  ev$OCC <- ifelse(ev$time < 144, 1, 2)
  ev$SELFADMIN <- as.numeric(ev$time < 144)
  dplyr::left_join(
    ev,
    dplyr::select(cohort, id, FFM, CONMED_METHAQUALONE, NAT2_SLOW, NAT2_RAPID, AGE, CREAT),
    by = "id"
  )
}

pk_day_exposure <- function(out) {
  out <- out[out$time >= 144, ]
  out |>
    dplyr::group_by(id) |>
    dplyr::summarise(auc = trap(time, Cc), cmax = max(Cc), .groups = "drop")
}

# Between-occasion variability on mean transit time is large (up to 94%), so
# the transit input of some doses is a narrow spike, and on the days before the
# PK day no observation grid constrains the solver's step. Each cohort is
# therefore re-solved with the same random effects and a 0.005 h maximum step;
# a dose the default solve stepped over would show up as a discrepancy.
solve_drug <- function(model, mg_per_tablet, drug) {
  ev <- cohort_events(mg_per_tablet)
  fit <- rxode2::rxSolve(model, ev)
  fine <- rxode2::rxSolve(model, ev, params = as.data.frame(fit$params),
                          hmax = 0.005, maxsteps = 1e7)
  a <- pk_day_exposure(as.data.frame(fit))
  b <- pk_day_exposure(as.data.frame(fine))
  out <- as.data.frame(fit)
  out <- out[out$time >= 143.99, ]
  out$tad <- pmax(out$time - 144, 0)
  out$drug <- drug
  list(
    sim = out[, c("id", "drug", "time", "tad", "Cc", "sim")],
    step_check = max(abs(a$auc / b$auc - 1), abs(a$cmax / b$cmax - 1))
  )
}

solved <- list(
  solve_drug(rif, 150, "Rifampicin"),
  solve_drug(inh, 75, "Isoniazid"),
  solve_drug(pza, 400, "Pyrazinamide"),
  solve_drug(emb, 275 * 0.74, "Ethambutol")
)
sims <- dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(solved, `[[`, "sim"))
step_check <- vapply(solved, `[[`, numeric(1), "step_check")

stopifnot(
  # Same random effects, default step versus 0.005 h: measured agreement is
  # about 1e-5 on PK-day AUC and Cmax; a skipped transit spike would differ by
  # a whole dose.
  all(step_check < 1e-3),
  n_subj <= 200,
  !anyNA(sims$Cc),
  # Fat-free mass and creatinine clearance land near the Table 1 medians.
  abs(stats::median(cohort$FFM) / 43.1 - 1) < 0.08,
  abs(stats::median(cohort$crcl_std) / 127.1 - 1) < 0.15
)
summary(cohort[, c("FFM", "AGE", "CREAT", "crcl_std")])
table(cohort$n_tab)
```

Individual peaks still span more than tenfold within each drug: a participant
whose ka draw falls in the lower tail of the 112-136% between-occasion
variability absorbs slowly and peaks low, which is a property of the model and
not of the solver (the step check above rules that out).

## Replicating Figure 1: visual predictive check

Figure 1 of the source is a VPC of the four drugs against time after the
observed dose. The percentiles below are of simulated observations including
residual error; as in the control streams, simulated values at or below the
LLOQ are set to half the LLOQ so the log axis stays finite.

```{r fig1, fig.height = 6, fig.cap = "Replicates Figure 1 of Wijk 2024: 5th, 50th and 95th percentiles of simulated concentrations against time after the observed steady-state dose."}
lloq <- c(Rifampicin = 0.117, Isoniazid = 0.105, Pyrazinamide = 0.2, Ethambutol = 0.0844)

vpc <- sims |>
  dplyr::filter(tad <= 8) |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    obs = ifelse(sim <= lloq[drug], lloq[drug] / 2, sim),
    tad = round(tad, 1)
  ) |>
  dplyr::group_by(drug, tad) |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    p05 = stats::quantile(obs, 0.05),
    p50 = stats::median(obs),
    p95 = stats::quantile(obs, 0.95),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  dplyr::mutate(drug = factor(drug, levels = names(lloq)))

ggplot(vpc, aes(tad)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = p05, ymax = p95), fill = "steelblue", alpha = 0.25) +
  geom_line(aes(y = p50), colour = "steelblue4", linewidth = 0.9) +
  facet_wrap(~drug, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_y_log10() +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(0, 1.5, 3, 5, 8)) +
  labs(x = "Time after dose (h)", y = "Concentration (mg/L)") +
  theme_bw()
```

The simulated medians follow the observed medians read from Figure 1: peaks
near 1.5 h of roughly 4-5 mg/L for rifampicin, 1.5 mg/L for isoniazid,
28 mg/L for pyrazinamide and 1.5 mg/L for ethambutol, with pyrazinamide and
ethambutol still well above the LLOQ before the next dose.

## NCA and comparison with Table 3

Table 3 of the source lists model-estimated Cmax and AUC0-24 for the study
participants (median and IQR). The simulated individual predictions over the
24 h after the observed dose are run through `PKNCA`.

```{r pknca}
nca_conc <- sims |>
  dplyr::filter(time >= 144, !is.na(Cc)) |>
  dplyr::mutate(treatment = drug) |>
  dplyr::select(id, treatment, tad, Cc)
nca_dose <- nca_conc |>
  dplyr::distinct(id, treatment) |>
  dplyr::mutate(tad = 0)

o_conc <- PKNCA::PKNCAconc(nca_conc, Cc ~ tad | treatment + id)
o_dose <- PKNCA::PKNCAdose(nca_dose, ~ tad | treatment + id)
intervals <- data.frame(start = 0, end = 24, cmax = TRUE, auclast = TRUE)
nca_res <- as.data.frame(PKNCA::pk.nca(PKNCA::PKNCAdata(o_conc, o_dose, intervals = intervals))$result) |>
  dplyr::filter(PPTESTCD %in% c("cmax", "auclast"))

stopifnot(nrow(nca_res) == 4 * n_subj * 2, !anyNA(nca_res$PPORRES))
```

```{r nca_compare}
published <- data.frame(
  treatment = c("Rifampicin", "Isoniazid", "Pyrazinamide", "Ethambutol"),
  cmax = c(5.29, 1.79, 30.0, 1.98),
  auclast = c(22.2, 7.53, 290, 13.2)
)
cmp <- nlmixr2lib::ncaComparisonTable(
  simulated = nca_res[, c("treatment", "PPTESTCD", "PPORRES")],
  reference = published,
  by = "treatment",
  params = c("cmax", "auclast"),
  tolerance_pct = 20
)
cmp |>
  dplyr::rename("Drug" = treatment) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

Cmax and AUC0-24 agree with Table 3 for all four drugs to within cohort noise.
The simulated pyrazinamide and ethambutol AUCs run about 10% above the
published medians across seeds, which is within what the assumed cohort
(height, creatinine, the weight-band split) can produce. The isoniazid AUC
median is the least stable row: the distribution is trimodal in NAT2
phenotype, so the median depends on the drawn share of slow acetylators. The
interquartile ranges show the spread is reproduced as well as the centre:

```{r nca_iqr}
sim_iqr <- nca_res |>
  dplyr::group_by(treatment, PPTESTCD) |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    median = stats::median(PPORRES),
    q25 = stats::quantile(PPORRES, 0.25),
    q75 = stats::quantile(PPORRES, 0.75),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
pub_iqr <- data.frame(
  treatment = rep(c("Rifampicin", "Isoniazid", "Pyrazinamide", "Ethambutol"), each = 2),
  PPTESTCD = rep(c("cmax", "auclast"), 4),
  published = c(
    "5.29 (3.53-6.88)", "22.2 (15.5-31.2)",
    "1.79 (1.19-2.27)", "7.53 (4.55-14.5)",
    "30.0 (25.8-33.5)", "290 (236-358)",
    "1.98 (1.42-2.44)", "13.2 (11.1-16.5)"
  )
)
iqr_table <- dplyr::left_join(pub_iqr, sim_iqr, by = c("treatment", "PPTESTCD")) |>
  dplyr::mutate(simulated = sprintf("%.3g (%.3g-%.3g)", median, q25, q75))

# Medians of a 150-participant cohort: a mis-transcribed clearance, dose or
# unit shifts these by tens of percent or more. Over ten seeds the realised
# differences ranged from -16% to +17% for every row except isoniazid AUC,
# which ranged from -3% to +27%: isoniazid AUC is trimodal in NAT2 phenotype,
# and the cohort median sits between the intermediate and slow modes, so it
# moves with the drawn share of slow acetylators. That row gets a wider bound.
ref_long <- tidyr::pivot_longer(published, -treatment, names_to = "PPTESTCD",
                                values_to = "ref")
chk <- dplyr::inner_join(sim_iqr, ref_long, by = c("treatment", "PPTESTCD"))
chk$pct_diff <- 100 * (chk$median / chk$ref - 1)
inh_auc <- chk$treatment == "Isoniazid" & chk$PPTESTCD == "auclast"
stopifnot(
  nrow(chk) == 8,
  all(abs(chk$pct_diff[!inh_auc]) < 25),
  abs(chk$pct_diff[inh_auc]) < 40
)

iqr_table |>
  dplyr::select(treatment, PPTESTCD, published, simulated) |>
  dplyr::mutate(PPTESTCD = ifelse(PPTESTCD == "cmax", "Cmax (mg/L)", "AUC0-24 (mg*h/L)")) |>
  dplyr::rename(
    "Drug" = treatment,
    "NCA parameter" = PPTESTCD,
    "Table 3 median (IQR)" = published,
    "Simulated median (IQR)" = simulated
  ) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

## Covariate effects

The retained covariates can be read off typical-value profiles. Methaqualone
users have the typical bioavailability of 1 and non-users 19.2% more, which
for a 450 mg rifampicin dose translates into a larger AUC ratio because
hepatic extraction saturates. Isoniazid exposure is ordered by NAT2 phenotype,
and ethambutol clearance changes by 2.6% for every 10 mL/min of standardised
creatinine clearance.

```{r covariate_effects}
rif_auc_meth <- vapply(c(0, 1), function(m) {
  p <- typical_last_interval(rif, 450, list(FFM = 43.4, OCC = 2, CONMED_METHAQUALONE = m),
                             n_dose = 7)
  trap(p$time, p$Cc)
}, numeric(1))

emb_cl_ratio <- vapply(c(97.1, 157.1), function(crcl) {
  creat <- (140 - 37) * 52 * 88.4 / (72 * crcl)
  p <- typical_last_interval(emb, 3 * 275 * 0.74,
                             list(FFM = 43.4, OCC = 2, AGE = 37, CREAT = creat))
  (3 * 275 * 0.74) / trap(p$time, p$Cc) / 48.8
}, numeric(1))

stopifnot(
  # Saturable extraction amplifies the 19.2% bioavailability difference.
  rif_auc_meth[1] / rif_auc_meth[2] > 1.192,
  # 1 +/- 0.00263624 * 30 mL/min.
  max(abs(emb_cl_ratio - c(1 - 0.0790872, 1 + 0.0790872))) < 1e-3
)
data.frame(
  effect = c(
    "Rifampicin AUC, no methaqualone / methaqualone (450 mg)",
    "Ethambutol CL at CrCl 97.1 / reference",
    "Ethambutol CL at CrCl 157.1 / reference"
  ),
  ratio = c(rif_auc_meth[1] / rif_auc_meth[2], emb_cl_ratio)
) |>
  dplyr::rename("Effect" = effect, "Ratio" = ratio) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3)
```

## Assumptions and deviations

**Control streams for structure, Table 2 for values.** The final NONMEM
control streams in the supplement and Table 2 agree for isoniazid,
pyrazinamide and ethambutol to the printed digits; for rifampicin the
control-stream `$THETA` values sit up to 0.3% from Table 2 (CLint,max * fu
42.4 vs 42.5 L/h, V 55.0 vs 55.1 L), and Table 2 is used. The variances are the
control-stream `$OMEGA` values; the square root of each reproduces the Table 2
percentage, which is therefore an omega standard deviation on the log scale,
not a coefficient of variation.

**Number of transit compartments.** The transit input in every control stream
is the Savic density with KTR = (NN + 1) / MTT. For isoniazid, pyrazinamide and
ethambutol, Table 2 prints NN + 1 (1, 3.73 and 3.01) while the control streams
carry NN = 0, 2.73 and 2.01, the latter two in blocks whose other values all
match Table 2. For rifampicin both say 17. The control-stream values are what
the estimates were obtained with, so they are used.

**Methaqualone is parameterised as the source wrote it.** The rifampicin
control stream takes methaqualone-positive participants as the reference
(`BIO_METHAQUALONE = 1`) and gives non-users `1 + 0.191955`. The Results
describe this as 19% lower bioavailability with methaqualone use; strictly,
users have 1 / 1.192 = 0.84 of the non-user bioavailability. The typical
values in Table 2 therefore describe a methaqualone user. The coefficient is
not listed in Table 2 and is taken from the control stream.

**Alcohol is not in the ethambutol model.** The Abstract and Results report
13% higher ethambutol clearance with high alcohol use (P = 0.002). The final
control stream has no alcohol term, Table 2 has no alcohol row, and the
P-value does not meet the P < 0.001 backward-elimination criterion of the
Methods, so the effect is documented in `covariatesDataExcluded` rather than
included. Adding it would raise ethambutol clearance by 13% in high-use
participants.

**Fat-free mass reference of 43.4 kg.** All four control streams normalise
allometry to `TVFFM = 43.4`; Table 2 footnote b names 43.1 kg, the Table 1
median. The control-stream value is used. The rifampicin control stream as
printed omits `WHSMAX = 37.99` in its female branch of the Janmahasatian
formula, which the other three include; the models take fat-free mass as a
covariate, so users should compute it with the full formula.

**Hepatic blood flow.** Table 2 prints QH as 73.9 L/h for rifampicin and
973.9 L/h for isoniazid. Footnote d states the hepatic parameters are 90 L/h
and 1 L for a 56.1 kg fat-free mass, and 90 x (43.1 / 56.1)^0.75 = 73.9, so
the isoniazid entry has a stray leading digit. Both control streams use
90 L/h scaled from 56.1 kg.

**Unbound fraction.** Both hepatic models report and estimate the product
CLint * fu (Table 2 footnote c). The control streams define fu (0.2 for
rifampicin, 0.95 for isoniazid) but never use it, so the models carry the
product directly and no separate fu parameter.

**Ethambutol creatinine clearance.** The control stream computes
Cockcroft-Gault clearance without the female factor and standardises it to
52 kg (`GFR_STD = GFR*52/WT`), so body weight cancels and the covariate depends
on age and serum creatinine only. The control-stream `$INPUT` does not list an
age column although the equation uses one; age is taken to be a data column.
Serum creatinine is not reported, so the cohort's distribution is assumed and
chosen to put the standardised clearance near the 127.1 mL/min centring value.

**Additive residual error.** Each control stream writes the additive standard
deviation as `THETA + 0.2 * LLOQ`. The theta is held at 0 for rifampicin,
isoniazid and ethambutol (0.0234, 0.021 and 0.0169 mg/L, printed as 0.02 in
Table 2) and estimated at 0.589 mg/L for pyrazinamide, giving 0.63 mg/L.
The M6 handling of BLQ data (an extra 50% of the LLOQ on imputed records) is an
estimation device and is not reproduced.

**Between-occasion variability.** Each control stream has two occasions with
one shared variance (`$OMEGA BLOCK(1)` then `SAME`); they are written as
two etas, the second fixed to the first's value, selected by `OCC`. Because the
occasion effect enters through indicator products rather than as a bare term
added to the log parameter, rxode2 warns that these etas are not
mu-referenced; this affects only the speed of a future estimation run, not
simulation. Between-subject variability exists only on clearance; the
zero-variance etas in the control streams are omitted.

**NAT2 mixture model.** Genotype was known for 33% of participants, and the
authors assigned a phenotype to the rest with a mixture model whose
probabilities were held at 36% / 40% / 24% (slow / intermediate / fast). That
is a device for missing data, so phenotype enters as the covariate pair
`NAT2_SLOW` / `NAT2_RAPID`, and the virtual cohort above draws it with the
mixture probabilities.

**Absorption is written out rather than delegated to `transit()`.** The control
streams set `F1 = 0` so the whole dose enters through the transit density. In
rxode2 the built-in `transit()` returns zero input once `f(depot)` is 0, so
the closed form is written out with `podo()` and `tad()`. Like the control
streams, it restarts with each dose, which loses nothing here because every
mean transit time is under an hour against a 24 h dosing interval; the
mass-balance checks above confirm it.

**Cohort.** Height, the split of weight within sex, age and serum creatinine
distributions are not reported and are assumed as described above. Race and
ethnicity are not reported beyond the South African study site.
